citation: 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2); 12 CFR pt. 1002, Supp. I, Comments 9(b)(2)-1 and 9(b)(2)-4; CFPB Circulars 2022-03 and 2023-03
reasoning: Listing the same four globally most important model features on every declined applicant's notice does not 'indicate the principal reason(s)' for that applicant's adverse action as 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2) requires, because Comment 9(b)(2)-4 requires the disclosed reasons to be the factors that most adversely affected the specific applicant's score, not a fixed list derived from the model's overall validation importance.

Ranking scored characteristics by how far the applicant's points fall below the average points achieved by applicants scoring at or slightly above the cutoff is one of the methods expressly approved in Official Interpretation 9(b)(2)-5 for selecting the principal reasons from a credit scoring system, that comment states the averages may be calculated during development of the system (so the 2021 figures are permissible), and disclosing the top four scored factors satisfies 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2)'s requirement that the reasons be specific and relate to the factors actually scored.

model_deciding_fact: Whether Ridgeway's maximum-points ranking method produces reasons substantially similar to those produced by the average-score methods described in comment 9(b)(2)-5.
reasoning: Comment 9(b)(2)-5 states that no single method of selecting reasons from a credit scoring system is required and describes two average-score methods (distance below the average of applicants at or slightly above the cutoff, or below the average of all applicants), accepting any other method only if it produces substantially similar results, so ranking by the gap below the maximum points available on each characteristic, which tends to overstate characteristics with wide point ranges that few applicants attain, complies only if Ridgeway can show it yields substantially similar reasons.

For an additive model each feature's SHAP value against an all-applicant development sample equals the applicant's component score minus the average component score of all applicants, so listing the four most negative contributions is the 'fell furthest below the average score achieved by all applicants, calculated during development' method that comment 9(b)(2)-4 accepts for identifying the principal reasons required by § 1002.9(b)(2).

Because the 655 score neither approved nor denied the application but referred it to judgmental review, the reasons must come from the factors the underwriter actually reviewed (comments 9(b)(2)-6 and 9(b)(2)-7), and 'Length of employment' specifically and accurately describes the job change two months earlier on which the underwriter relied, satisfying § 1002.9(b)(2).

Because the applicant passed the scorecard (742 versus a 700 line) and was denied only on the underwriter's judgmental finding that income could not be verified, comment 9(b)(2)-7 requires that the disclosed reasons relate to the factors reviewed judgmentally, and padding the notice with 'Number of recent inquiries' and 'Length of credit history' drawn from the scorecard component the applicant did not fail misstates the principal reasons for the adverse action in violation of 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2).

Under comment 9(b)(2)-7, when an application falls into a gray band and is denied after a judgmental assessment the disclosed reasons must come from both the scoring and judgmental components, and comment 9(b)(2)-4 forbids excluding any principal reason, so dropping the underwriter's 'Unable to verify income' because the notice template has only four lines violates 1002.9(b)(2); the four-reason figure in comment 9(b)(2)-1 is guidance on helpfulness, not a cap that justifies omitting a principal reason from one component.

Section 1002.9(b)(2) requires the statement to indicate the principal reason(s), and comment 9(b)(2)-4 provides that no factor that was a principal reason may be excluded from disclosure, so a policy of listing only the single largest shortfall when three other characteristics have shortfalls of 21, 19 and 18 points (within four points of the top one) omits factors that were plainly principal reasons, even though comment 9(b)(2)-1 contemplates disclosing up to four.

reasoning: Where a creditor elects under 12 CFR 1002.9(c)(1)(i) to take adverse action on an incomplete application rather than send a notice of incompleteness, 'Credit application incomplete' is a specific statement of the principal reason that satisfies 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2), as reflected by its inclusion as a listed reason on sample Form C-1, because the missing pay stubs were in fact the reason for the denial.

citation: 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2); 12 CFR 1002.9(a)(2); 12 CFR 1002.9(g); Official Interpretation comment 9(g)-1; comment 9(b)(2)-2

reasoning: Both reasons ('Excessive obligations in relation to income' and 'Limited credit experience') are specific factors rather than the prohibited 'internal standards or policies' or 'failed to achieve a qualifying score' statements, and because the applicant used no credit from any bank each of the three must give notice directly or through the platform, which properly names each creditor under 1002.9(g); but comment 9(g)-1 requires a single notice given on behalf of several creditors to state the principal reasons each creditor relied on and to clearly indicate which reasons relate to which creditor (or instead disclose the right to request reasons within 30 days), and the facts do not establish that the two reasons are attributed to, and were actually the principal reasons of, each bank.

The loan officer's statement that the application was declined because the applicant's monthly debt payments were too high relative to income is a specific principal reason (the familiar 'excessive obligations in relation to income' ground) rather than a bare reference to internal standards or a failed credit score, so it satisfies the specificity requirement of 1002.9(b)(2); and because Prairie State Bank received no more than 150 applications in the preceding calendar year (140), 1002.9(d) allows the notice and statement of specific reasons to be given orally, and the call two weeks after the decision fell within the 30-day window of 1002.9(a)(1)(i), so the absence of a written notice does not create a violation.

Section 1002.9(b)(2) governs only the content of a statement of reasons once one is furnished, and here none has been given or requested; because the bakery had gross revenues of $1 million or less, Oakmont's oral notice of the decline and its application-time disclosure of the right to request reasons within 60 days (with the office's name, address and telephone number and the ECOA notice) are expressly permitted by 1002.9(a)(3)(i)(A)-(B), so no statement subject to the (b)(2) specificity requirement is yet due and nothing insufficient has been provided (if the owner requests within 60 days, Oakmont must then state the specific principal reasons rather than merely that the model declined or a qualifying score was not met).

The notice states two specific principal reasons, 'Excessive obligations in relation to income' and 'Limited credit experience', rather than a bare reference to internal standards or a failed credit score, which is what 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2) requires; the applicant's non-acceptance of the counteroffer and the absence of any later notice do not bear on the specificity of the reasons under (b)(2).

Under 12 CFR 1002.9(g), when an application is made on the applicant's behalf to more than one creditor and the applicant expressly accepts or uses credit offered by one of them (here the buyer signed and was financed under Bank A's retail installment contract), notification of action taken by the other creditors is not required, so Banks B, C and D owed no adverse action notice and the specific-reasons requirement of 1002.9(b)(2), which attaches only to a statement of reasons required by 1002.9(a)(2)(i), was never triggered.

citation: 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2); Supplement I to Part 1002, comments 9(b)(2)-2 and 9(b)(2)-4

citation: 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2); 12 CFR 1002.2(c)(2)(ii); Supplement I to Part 1002, comment 2(c)(2)(ii)-2

citation: 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2); 12 CFR 1002.2(c)(1)(i); Supplement I comment 2(c)(1)(i)-1; Supplement I comment 9(b)(2)-2

citation: 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2); 12 CFR 1002.9(a)(1)(ii); Comment 9(a)(1)-3; Comment 9(a)(1)-4; Appendix C, Form C-1
reasoning: Where the application is incomplete in information the applicant can supply and the creditor lacks enough data to decide (its model cannot score without income), comment 9(a)(1)-3 expressly permits denial citing incompleteness, and the timely notice with that reason (a listed reason on Form C-1) meets § 1002.9(b)(2).

model_deciding_fact: Whether Meridian lacked sufficient data for a credit decision without the two pay stubs (so the incompleteness was the actual reason for the decline), or already had enough information to decide and declined on some other ground.

Closing one cardholder's account is a termination that is not class-wide and therefore adverse action under 1002.2(c)(1)(ii), the delinquency exclusion in 1002.2(c)(2)(ii) does not apply because the account was no longer delinquent (comment 2(c)(2)(ii)-2 says notice is generally required when the action rests on a past delinquency), so Northgate had to notify within 30 days under 1002.9(a)(1)(iii) with a statement of specific principal reasons meeting 1002.9(b)(2), and sending no notice at all means no compliant statement of reasons was given.

seam: S4 ECOA reasons vs FCRA key factors

A score of 655 fell in the gray band (620 to 699) and the underwriter then denied after a judgmental review, so comment 9(b)(2)-7 requires the disclosed reasons to come from both the scored component and the judgmental component, yet the notice lists only the judgmental factor ('Length of employment') and omits the scorecard shortfalls on revolving utilization and recent inquiries, contrary to 1002.9(b)(2) and comment 9(b)(2)-4 (no principal reason may be excluded).

Because the denial rested on a score below the cutoff and the notice lists the four scored characteristics with the largest shortfalls, it satisfies § 1002.9(b)(2) and comments 9(b)(2)-4 and -5, which require reasons to relate only to factors actually scored, so the unscored 2023 charge-off need not be disclosed.

seam: S12 reasons given on request / third-party notices
reasoning: Comment 9(g)-1 requires a single third-party notice that gives reasons to clearly indicate which reasons relate to which creditor, but this notice pools both reasons across all three banks, so it does not accurately state each bank's actual principal reason as 1002.9(b)(2) and comment 9(b)(2)-2 require (it implies Banks B and C relied on excessive obligations and Bank A on limited credit experience).

citation: 12 CFR 1002.9(b)(2); Supp. I comments 9(b)(2)-2 and 9(b)(2)-3; Appendix C, Form C-1 ('Unable to verify income') and instruction 4
reasoning: Because the model actually takes both stated income and the bureau-derived estimate as inputs, the notice's reason (stated income inconsistent with estimated income) names a specific factor actually considered, much like the sample reason 'unable to verify income', which satisfies the specific and accurate reasons standard of 1002.9(b)(2) and comment 9(b)(2)-2 and 9(b)(2)-3 without needing to explain how the factor hurt the applicant.

Closing a credit card account because of a delinquency on that same account is an action relating to delinquency on the account that is excluded from 'adverse action' by 1002.2(c)(2)(ii) and comment 2(c)(2)(ii)-2 (and (c)(3) makes the exclusion govern), so no statement of specific reasons is required under 1002.9(a)(2) or (b)(2) and the generic 'account-management policy' wording is not a violation, assuming the delinquency was current rather than a cured past delinquency.

model_deciding_fact: Whether the Northgate credit agreement explicitly provided for terminating the account when the cardholder moves out of the service area.
reasoning: Under comment 2(c)(1)(ii)-1 a termination because the cardholder moved out of the service area is adverse action unless the credit agreement explicitly provided for it, and if it is adverse action then 'in accordance with our account policies' is an insufficient internal-policy statement under 1002.9(b)(2), whereas if the agreement expressly allowed it there is no adverse action and no statement of reasons is required.

A request to extend the remaining term of a loan made through the creditor's own modification form is adverse action when refused (§ 1002.2(c)(1)(i); comment 2(c)(1)(i)-1), and telling the borrower that modifications are 'handled at our discretion' is a bare statement of internal policy that gives no specific principal reason, which § 1002.9(b)(2) says is insufficient.
